utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, the Chamber reminds you that you are still bound by the declaration you made to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness was still being led under direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me and understand me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, could you describe Milan Martic's office, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a very big office, like 20 metres square, so we were feeling rather cramped when we sat down at the table. On the opposite side, Mr. Martic sat down, and I think he was wearing his ceremonial uniform, not a camouflage uniform. A ceremonial uniform means a white shirt with a tie. His desk was opposite from us, between two pillars, and next to him was a very large man wearing a camouflage uniform and a gun, and he was such a big man, so tall, that we were all fascinated. He was sitting behind Martic's back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you were fascinated. Can you describe what impression Mr. Martic made on you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what should I tell you? This whole procedure, the body search, the way they escorted us upstairs, the way they introduced us to him, we all agreed later within our group that Martic wanted to create the impression of being the man who has everything under control, who has to approve everything, who has to give his permission for us to do our job in that territory, a man who has to be obeyed, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us what -- what was discussed at the meeting? What did -- and in particular, what did Milan Martic say to you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first like to mention that Martic gave us a briefing about the situation in the area, the number of the population, the area that his police is covering, the problems that had arisen. That was the background he gave. And then he gave us a briefing about the political and security situation in that territory. And speaking about the political aspect, he said that the Serb people had expressed their readiness and willingness not to live in Croatia and that they were united in this demand, that they wanted instead to live within Yugoslavia, and if they had -- if they were to continue to live in Croatia under the pro-Ustasha government of Mr. Tudjman, they would be a minority, that he was not about to allow Krajina to become a repetition of the Jasenica concentration camp from the World War II, that the Serbs of Krajina wanted to live in one single country with all the other Serbs from Yugoslavia, including Serbia, and that by no means would the Serb people live under the Ustasha authorities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The concentration camp was called Jasenovac, not Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in that last answer you used the term -- in describing what Milan Martic said on that occasion you used the term Ustasha on several occasions. Did Milan Martic use that term in talking about the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't use the term Ustasha describing the government, but he talked about the Ustasha system, Ustasha structures, and the Ustasha people, men. He said that Tudjman was a former general of the JNA who had allowed some notorious Ustashas to become members of his government, of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Martic about your discussions with -- that you had had with the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taking the chair while giving us this briefing about the general situation, and he also said that the Serb people had expressed their readiness and desire to establish some sort of district or region that would unite all Serbs in Croatia and enable them to protect their interests because they didn't want to be a minority in Croatia. Instead, they wanted to live in a unified state of Yugoslavia with all other Serbs. Mr. Martic used the word "Yugoslavia" a lot, and our group was a bit taken aback by that, because there was not a single Yugoslav emblem in his office. There were some photos of some historic Serbian figures like St. Sava, and even that was on calendars. And I said on of my group, "There's nothing Yugoslav around here." And Mr. Martic said, "Does that bother you?" And we didn't comment on that any more, because after all, we were on a peace mission. Later on, the leader of our group, number 2, described our mission and our tasks and said that the previous day we had a meeting at the MUP, the Ministry of Interior of Sibenik. And I apologise in advance if I cause some confusion now, because the word "secretariat" had already been replaced in Sibenik by the word "ministry." The term "secretariat" was associated at that time with Belgrade. Anyway, the lead are of our group said that we had met with a deputy of the Croatian minister who briefed us on the current situation in all of Croatia and said, among other things, that their main problem was Krajina and the Serbs living there, especially those following Martic. And as the deputy minister put it, Martic had established some sort of parapolice force that acted independently of the laws of Croatia, which they did not recognise. And the lead are of our group, number 2 on this list, told Martic all this. He also said that the Croatian deputy minister offered Martic the job of the Secretary of Interior in Knin in exchange for his commitment to act within the laws of the Croatian state. The leader of our group also said that assistance was available to us from the army and the Croatian authorities because the position of our group was that we were on an official mission on the territory of Croatia. At that point, Martic told us that as far as the Autonomous Region of Krajina is concerned, we had to address him for assistance because if we went out into the field on our own, we could get into trouble and that he was responsible for our safety on the territory of SAO Krajina. It was a preliminary meeting designed to give us an opportunity to describe to him our mission and our purpose, because we were supposed to contact each of the conflicting parties in that region and to try to prevent incidents. That was the gist of that meeting. If I omitted something, it must be a minor detail. After all, so many years have passed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. That was a very thorough and complete answer. I do have a couple of questions about what you've told us. Specifically, what was Martic's reaction, if any, to what you told him about the offer from the Croatian authorities that he could become the -- the Secretary of Interior in Knin in exchange for his commitment to act within the laws of the Croatian state? How did he react to that, if he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the very outset when he told us about his role and his position there, and when he said that the Serb people would no longer live in Croatia, that he was there to protect the Serbian people and to organise the police force, made it very clear that we could expect no other answer from him. He had already established a police force to protect Serb people, because they were in danger, not the Croatian people. Whatever he said later, it was in that same context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've described that Milan Martic briefed you on -- on what was happening in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or the SAO Krajina, and about his role in organising the police force. Did you learn then or later whether Milan Martic had control over the entire police within the SAO Krajina or just part of the police? Did you learn anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had organised that police force as a united police force for the whole of SAO Krajina. And now I'm remembering that we told him -- we remarked upon the fact that he had dismissed some ethnic Croat policemen, and to that he responded that every police officer could stay on the force as long as he respected the laws of Yugoslavia. At that point, Krajina did not have a separate legislation. That sounded rather odd to us, because even while Yugoslavia existed, each republic had its own legislation, and there was no law in Serbia that could be enforced in Croatia and vice versa. Anyway, he said that any police officer willing to observe the of Yugoslavia could stay on the force, which the Croat officers didn't want to do, and that's why they had to go. They had to leave the Secretariat of the Interior in Knin. And he went on to say that there was a shortage of staff and that's why he was forced to organise the reserve police force in certain places. And the task of the reservists was to help citizens organise their defence in Serb-populated areas. But on the ground it was rather impossible, because you had one Serb village, then one Croatian, then two Serb villages, then another Croatian, and it wasn't clear what kind of defence organisation he meant. Maybe village guards or barricades or checkpoints that we later saw on the ground, but it was organised with the help of the Secretariat of the Interior in Knin. That much we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to be sure I'm clear on your answer at the beginning here. You said when I asked you if Martic had control over the whole police, you said, "He said that he had organised that police force as a united police force for the whole of SAO Krajina." Just to be clear, are you saying there that Milan Martic had control over all of the police in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then I just want to clarify what may have been either a slip of the tongue or a translation error in your answer. You were telling us about how Milan Martic talked about how he wanted the laws of Yugoslavia to be enforced in the SAO Krajina, and then you said, "That sounded rather odd to us because even while Yugoslavia existed, each republic had its own legislation, and there was no law in Serbia that could be enforced in Croatia and vice versa." Did you mean Serbia or Yugoslavia in that part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to make it clearer. It might take some time though. Yugoslav legislation was of a general nature, and it applied to all six republics and two autonomous provinces. Within that legislative framework, each republic adopted its own laws depending on its own needs and requirements to protect its interests, be it the Criminal Code or some other legislation. But every republic had its own legislation, whereas the Yugoslav legislation had the character of legislative framework, an instruction or a guideline for enacting republic laws, and it was odd to hear Martic emphasise Yugoslavia and Yugoslav interests at that time, that the Serb people wanted to continue living in Yugoslavia rather than Croatia. He would use the terms "Yugoslavia" and "Serbia" interchangeably sometimes, but clearly after the secession of other republics, which left only Serbia and Montenegro, it became clear what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in that meeting was there any discussion about the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was said at the meeting that Serb people had organised themselves of their own accord in some places where they thought they were in danger, that Serb forces, with the help of the police, organised those night guards and checkpoints on roads leading to Serb-populated areas. And indeed, we saw that later on the ground. On the other hand, it's true that Croats organised those same guards and checkpoints in Croat-populated places. It may sound bizarre because there were many mixed settlements and there was a whole lot of those barricades and checkpoints. The barricades were sometimes heaps of rocks or signs saying that Croats or Serbs, depending on which side erected that were not allowed to pass. And on both sides there were policemen wearing uniforms. Some wore civilian clothes, but all carried weapons. When they saw us coming, they tried to throw their guns into the nearest brush or shrubbery, and the whole situation was a bit ridiculous, and it made our role a bit farcical as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, at that meeting was there any discussion about visiting areas within the SAO Krajina and about how that would be done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Martic himself demanded that we visit the hot spots of crisis where some sort of incident between Serbs and Croats was expected to occur any minute. Bratiskovac, Kistanje, Rupe are some of the place names. Cetinje. On the Benkovac side there was Benkovac and Obrovac. But at the beginning, at least, I was in charge of Knin. And I only ever visited Benkovac once or twice, so I couldn't tell you any more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about, when you -- when you visited these areas, whether you would be allowed to do it on your own or whether you would have to have somebody with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In those areas that Martic held under his control, we had to be escorted by his police for our own safety and in order to be able to assess the situation on the ground. That's what he said. At any rate, we didn't go anywhere alone. However, when there were incidents between JNA members and the populous, we would not inform Martic. And when we visited Serb-populated villages and hamlets, we didn't go through Martic because Knin was not at all on the way, and it would take a long time to go back to Knin, get his approval or assistance and then go back to the village. But as far as Knin is concerned, and as far as I am concerned, I would always first go to the secretariat to see Martic or one of his men and to get them to accompany me on my visit to wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever have contact with a man by the name of Milenko Zelenbaba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was he at that time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his official position was. Three or four times I went towards Cetinje, Kistanje, Kijevo with him. We tried to avoid asking a lot of questions but just accompanying him around I was able to see what his role was. It seems to me he was one of the leading people in Knin, and most likely he had been in charge of Civljani and Cetinje because they had a police station there. I saw that the people knew him there and called him commander, komandir, so most likely he had been the commander of the police station there. On the three occasions we went out on the ground together to calm down conflicts between Kijevo and Civljani, Cetinje, Vrlike, because there were barricades there we had to go and remove them. We would do that by say, and at night they would erect the barricades again. And so it went on day by day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what relationship Milenko Zelenbaba had with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that because I did not have occasion to see them together, but most probably Zelenbaba was subordinate to Milan Martic, because whenever I said there was a problem there and I had to go there, Zelenbaba would receive orders from his superior, Martic, to accompany me on the ground. However, I did not see for myself their interaction. For a time, I saw Zelenbaba. Later on I didn't see him in uniform any more or in the police station, so I can't say what happened to him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, on Friday you described for us how the ministries of the interior at the federal level and the republic level were organised into a public security branch and a state security branch. Do you know if Milan Martic organised the Ministry of the Interior or the Secretariat of the Interior, I should say, in Knin in the same way, having a public security branch and a state security branch? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the organisation within the secretariat, in my conversations with my colleagues, we commented among ourselves that on the territory of the SAO Krajina and Knin, Martic had also organised a constituent security service. It was my colleagues who went there more often who said that -- or, rather, those who contacted Martic more often. But we would always comment on this among ourselves when we returned to our base. We would go for a walk outside the hotel to comment on the events of the day. We also remarked on the fact that the State Security Service of Serbia had got involved in organising the State Security Service on the territory of the SAO Krajina. On one or two occasions I saw Stanisic in Knin, but only in passing. This was something I saw when I went to see Branko Polizota. On the third or fourth day of my stay in the Krajina, in Sibenik I went to see him, and he said that they had information that the Serbian service - I am quoting his words - "Was involved in activities in the SAO Krajina. This would mean we always used the acronym to describe that service. Branko Polizota told me that Serbia had organised the work of the state security on the territory of the SAO Krajina. At first I did not believe this, but later on my colleagues from my group confirmed this in our conversations, and I myself saw Stanisic in Knin on one or two occasions. We said hello in passing. And then I saw him around a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the transcript on the monitor any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We have just been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we're become in open session, so please take care not to mention names. Now, with respect to the various conflict areas that you have spoken about, were you able to observe what the role of the JNA was, if any, when these conflicts occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was located at all those points that could become hotbeds of crisis or were already hotbeds of crisis, and they had their mobile units fully equipped and fully armed in that area. Our mission was to protect the population on both sides, and we had no authority over the area in order to tell them where to deploy their forces. But at the request of citizens, we could intervene in case of incidents between the population and the army, only with a view to protecting the population, not with any authority to influence with the position of the JNA or their location in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, excuse me, maybe I wasn't clear or there was something with the interpretation. I wasn't asking about what your role was with respect to the JNA. What I was interested in was you -- excuse me. Were you able to observe what the -- when these conflicts erupted that you talked about and that you would go visit the area, would you able to observe what did the JNA do with respect to these conflicts? What role did they play with respect to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended on the situation on the ground and the area and the incidents that occurred between the two ethnicities. The army would position themselves between the sides. That's at least what happened at the very beginning. Later on, we talked among ourselves within the group and remarked upon the fact that the army was in a way determining the boundaries of SAO Krajina by positioning themselves on certain lines, and we witnessed that on the ground. If there was an incident, a clash between one village and another and barricades were set up, the army would come in immediately and set up their checkpoint. At the beginning, around Knin, Croats had their own checkpoint and barricade outside Drnis. First there was a police checkpoint outside the village, and then 500 metres ahead there would be another barricade manned by Croat volunteers or the ZNG, and they were hidden purportedly defending this border. The army was not present there at the beginning. Still further up there would be a Serb barricade. But later on when the SAO Krajina began to develop as a political entity, JNA started setting up its own checkpoints. At first they were not formal checkpoints. The army would simply set up their tents and control traffic, entries and exits from the SAO Krajina. They would list all the vehicles and all the persons that crossed that boundary. That lasted for a couple of months this activity of the JNA when they were creating the borders of the SAO Krajina. And towards the end of our mission, our group commented on the fact that the JNA was doing that. We were not able to say with certainty whether the JNA was trying to -- to determine the boundaries of this region or to protect the Serb population. We couldn't tell. Although it's true that both in the area of Croatia and the area of SAO Krajina there were military checkpoints and military units stationed, for instance, overlooking Rupe, there was a military presence and the army was fully equipped in combat terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in that answer you said when you were talking about the army setting up their tents and checkpoints, you said that lasted for a couple of months this activity of the JNA when they were creating the borders of the SAO Krajina, and then you said, "Towards the ends of our submission." So did you say a couple of months and, if so, what months are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you which months, but at the beginning there were military checkpoints but only mobile ones. There would be a vehicle, a couple of soldiers and one officer. And these checkpoints were mobile. However, later on there were standing checkpoints manned by troops who had their tents nearby because they had to sleep somewhere. I can only tell you about the time that we spent there. I cannot tell you about the later months, because I wasn't there to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I wanted to get clear on. Okay. Now, I want to ask you about -- about the -- if you could describe the Serb checkpoints, please. Can you tell us -- or barricades as -- could you tell us how -- how were they manned? What people were at the check -- at the barricades on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the barricades would be manned for the most part by local people, and there would be some reserve policemen in uniform, some sort of blue uniform. In fact, that was the regular police uniform. However, major checkpoints such as the one in Civljani would also be manned on the Serb side by policemen in camouflage uniforms. Between Drnis and Kosovo Polje there was a major Serb checkpoint. Most of the men were in police uniforms. And we could notice that some of the men were dressed in regular uniforms, whereas other men seemed to be dressed in uniforms that they had borrowed and that didn't fit them, and we thought that they were local -- local people who just got hold of a uniform. Our vehicle, I must say, was conspicuous, so that every time reservists would withdraw and the local men would come forward and would say that, "We are local people. We are just defending the Serb people," and we pretended that we hadn't noticed anything. And they really did feel they were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you observe any signs or posters at the Serb barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, especially around Skradin, in hamlets populated by Serbs, barricades were set up and signs "This is SAO Krajina," "Martic, we are with you," "Long live the Serbian people," "Long live SAO Krajina," "We are united," all sorts of slogans, drawings, the cross with the four S's, but all that was in the hamlets where the checkpoints were set by local people with the help of Martic's police. In larger places where traffic was busier, they didn't put up these signs. Around Bratiskovac, around Skradin, Kistanje, you could see those signs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, at these barricades did you ever talk to the Martic's Police about removing the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the purpose of our mission. We had to talk to the local people, the villages, and we told them that, first of all, it was illegal for them to put those barricades, that they should instead try to ensure a peaceful co-existence and cooperation with the Croats. The policemen wore sleeve patches with the inscription "Martic's Police." And we talked to them as well. They were cooperative in contacts with us. They said they would try and get it across to the local residents that they should not put up these barricades and not behave in that way, but it was all empty talk. And as soon as we turned our backs, none of that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us before that you went to -- on one occasion you went to Benkovac and you went to Obrovac. Can you tell us what you saw in Benkovac and Obrovac, where you went and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion I went there with my leader, under number 2, because I was not familiar with that terrain. Of course, he had his own driver and his own escort, so there were four of us in the car. As soon as we got to the centre of the village, we would get out, visit the police station. We found several policemen there. We would discuss the problems with them. They would refrain from entering into arguments or discussing the real issues on the ground but would always refer us back to Martic. We saw then that the sign on the building had been removed and changed. The citizens would show us that as well, saying, "You see? We are in power here. We have our own authorities here, our own organs." The policemen, though, refrained from entering into any kind of discussion, although we insisted and kept asking questions, asking about the situation on the ground, but they evaded our questions and kept referring us back to Martic, telling us he was the one who would inform us about the situation on the ground the same thing happened in Benkovac and Obrovac. I was there once or twice, but it was purely a waste of time. We didn't achieve any goals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are you able to recall how the sign changes on the police station in Benkovac and Obrovac? You said they had taken down the old sign and put up the new sign and said, "You see? We are in power here." What was the change in the sign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't there when the change was made, but you could see the traces on the building because the signs were not the same size. The previous sign had been bigger, so the colour was different around it. It used to be OU -- well, what it said was, the new sign, what the new sign said was "OUP," meaning the organ or the Department of the Interior, and then it said, "SAO Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the session please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Milan Martic said about the prisoners and about the topic of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we told him that Vukosic had said that the Croatian side was ready for an exchange of prisoners and we proposed that Martic accept that, he immediately opposed it. He said that they were all members of the ZNG, that they had been arrested while under arms at the barricades and the lines, that they were pro-Ustasha, pro-Croatian. He wanted to show that they were guilty, that they had been captured as members of the ZNG while armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he tell you what was going to happen to these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, his reply was negative. He said they would be tried before a court of Yugoslavia as members of the ZNG and as fighters of Croatian paramilitary units, that they would have them tried, and that the court's judgement would be carried out. He, on that day, did not accept any exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was your reaction when he told you that they would be tried before a court of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We let him know that they could not be tried before a Yugoslav court, that they could only be tried before a Croatian court or the court of some other republic, not of Yugoslavia. They could be tried before a Serbian court. But Yugoslavia did not have its legislation, and it did not have its courts as a federation. It was the republics who had courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- and did he have any response to that when you told him that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that in any case, they would be tried because they were members of the ZNG, because they had carried weapons, they had been at the barricades and the lines where they had been arrested, and he rejected any exchange of prisoners. No numbers of prisoners were mentioned either by Vukosic or by Martic. It was always all for all. And we didn't even know how many prisoners there were on each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Martic about where the prisoners were being held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because Vukosic had told us that there was no prison -- there were no facilities in Knin for detention. And we asked where he was keeping the prisoners. He said that there were several premises where prisoners could be kept pursuant to all the regulations of the laws of war. We did not insist on him showing us those premises, and he showed no desire to let us see those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- the next day did you have a meeting with the person who is at number 10 on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: (redacted) Again, he insisted at that we try again, that we try to get this exchange. He said he was afraid for the lives of the prisoners and the conditions they were living in because, as far as he knew, there were no appropriate facilities in Knin. He was afraid they might be maltreated by Martic's police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just have a redaction at the sentence that's on my line 3 of page -- no, sorry, line 2 of page 42, the sentence starting "On the next day."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the sentence starting "On the next day," at line 2 of page 42, please be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after that did you have any further meetings with Milan Martic on this topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day after our meeting with person number 10, or the very next day, we again went to see Milan Martic. I went with person number 4, and we were to discuss this issue. We did not find Martic in his office, so we waited a little. We were told by some of his men that Martic would not be in on at that day, that he was busy. So we used the time to tour Knin, and then we went back not having finished the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did meet with Milan Martic on this topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the very next day after this unsuccessful visit. I went again with person number 4, and on that occasion we did find Martic in his office. Since we were authorised by person number 2 to present our demands more strongly and to insist with Mr. Martic, we did so. We managed to persuade Martic to agree to the exchange, which at first he opposed. He waved his hand and said, "All right. Organise it." And then he appointed a person with whom we were to agree the technical details of the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the exchange subsequently take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, on the day after that. On the previous day we had agreed the method and time. Perhaps I said it was around noon, but now I remember it was 4.00 p.m., 1600 hours, because I can now connect it with some subsequent events which took place after the exchange. We agreed to have the exchange at 1600 hours at Kosovo Polje. They were to fly a white flag above the checkpoint held by Martic's policemen, and we would also fly a white flag on the checkpoint held by the Croatian police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many prisoners were exchanged at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, an hour and a half or two hours prior to the exchange, I and person number 4 took over two prisoners, and person number 10 had another two in the car. We then set out towards Drnis or, rather, the agreed spot in Kosovo Polje. I remember that we talked along the way, and one of the prisoners said his name was Plavso. I talked to him. He said he had been born in Knin. The other one was from a village in the vicinity. I no longer recall the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So there were four prisoners brought from the Croatian side, and they were exchanged for how many prisoners from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I and person number 4. I apologise. I and person number 4 took those four persons, and as there was a distance between the checkpoint held bit Croats and the checkpoint held by Martic's police, we stopped halfway between the two. And then Martic's police brought four persons in civilian clothes. We greeted Martic's policemen with the prisoners, thanked them and everybody was polite.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we redact that first line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the first line -- first sentence of line 2 at

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, after the prisoner exchange did you have occasion to talk to any of the prisoners that had been held in Knin and had just been released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, we took two prisoners in our car where my colleague and I were, and two went with person number 10. We brought them to Drnis, to the police station in Drnis. Along the way I asked the man where he was from, one of them, and he said he was a Croat from Knin, that he had been arrested two days previously in front of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That one who said he had been arrested two days previously in front of his house, could you tell how old he was, or did he tell you how old he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time was short, I mean the time of the drive. We did not spend a lot of time together. I think it's less than a kilometre. All he said was that he had been arrested two days previously in front of his house, that he had never participated in any Croatian units. He showed me, lifting up his T-shirt, how he had been beaten and maltreated by Martic's men in the prison. He told me they had been held in the basement of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When he lifted up his T-shirt, were you able to see anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw bruises on his back. He said that he had been beaten by Martic's policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did the other man, the other prisoner who had been released, did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat that the drive was very brief. It was less than a kilometre. We didn't have much time. Later on we learned because both sides were concealing the real truth from us. We learned from person 10 that he knew that there were three prisoners, not four, when we went see person 10 on the next day talking about the exchange, he said, "I didn't know about the fourth man. I knew about three." And I said, "Why didn't you tell us?" And he said, "Well, if I told you that, I would have to tell you how many I had." That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did either of the prisoners in your car tell you anything about the conditions under which they had been detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same prisoner told me that he had been in the basement of the building, that the conditions had been very bad, that he had been given some sandwiches to eat, that he was interrogated every day. The entire conversation took five or six minutes, as long as it took to drive to the Drnis police station where we handed them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did person number 10 later tell you anything about what the other two prisoners had said or what he had observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything. They didn't want to share information with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So did you learn anything about what had happened with the other two prisoners in terms of their detention, their conditions of detention, or where they had been detained, or anything that had happened to them while they were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next day when we went to see person number 10, he thought we knew where Martic was holding prisoners, and he said, "Did you see that room?" And we said, "No." And he said, "Well, the conditions are unbearable. It's a basement. It's dirty. It's damp." He said, "I don't know how he managed to transform that area into a detention unit, because the conditions were very bad," and that was the end of the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, during your time that you were in the area, during that approximately one month or so, did you have any meetings with Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our group as a whole did not have a meeting. On one occasion I, when visiting the terrain with person number 2, plus a driver and a security man, when we were in Knin we set out towards Sinj, to the place where Milan Babic was born, and person number 2 said it would be a good idea to see him and discuss the situation with him. We found his mother there, and she told us he wasn't there. We asked some neighbours, and they also said that he wasn't there, that he hadn't been home for two days. So we went back not having seen him. I will really wasn't told by number 2 what the purpose of that trip had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just the last question before the break. Can you tell us why didn't you try to have a more formal official meeting with Milan Babic the way you had done so with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milan Babic was a political figure. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time for the break. Out of an abundance of caution, I think it would be prudent to redact the sentence -- the second sentence of the answer, the last answer, "We were members."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "We were members"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the second sentence of the last answer. It starts off as, "We were members," and I don't want to read the rest of it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the sentence in the last answer starting with "We were members" please be redacted. It will start at line 6 on page 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I think this is a convenient time, Your Honour, for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court will adjourn, and we will reconvene at half past twelve. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we're still in open session, so if you could refer to your sheet if you're referring to any names. If you could remember. Thank you. I want to ask you about a new topic now. Did there come a time when refugees appeared in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. I can't remember the exact date, but it was around the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened on that date? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning when I left my room and went into the lobby of the hotel, I saw a large group of people strangely dressed, carrying bags, plastic bags, suitcases. Some of them were in the lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you find out who these people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go to the reception desk, and I asked the receptionist -- rather, the chief of reception, a man called Ivica, who they were. I did not assume they were refugees. I asked who they were, whether they were staying at the hotel or what, and then the gentleman told me that those people are Croats, refugees from Knin and that area. He told me that a lot of them were put up at the hotel, he said something around 600, whereas others were placed in other hotels or with their own relatives. But he said that all Croats had left the so-called SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you that day or the next day have a conversation with the person who is number 10 about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with person number 10 on a daily basis, and we had an office allocated to us in the building of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, and we would either run into each other on the way there, or we would agree to have a coffee together. I don't know about that period after the refugees appeared, whether we talked to them together, but I did talk to them on my own. I interviewed a lot of people and asked them what they had fled from, who they had fled from. I had the impression that if we had worked individually, people would accuse us of being -- of siding with one or the other side. I met with person number 10 the next day in connection with this issue, and I and person number 3 went to the place of person number 10 to talk about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did person number 10 tell you, if anything, about these refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He informed us that there was a large number of refugees, Croat refugees, from the area of SAO Krajina. All those who were physically able to leave Krajina did so. Only elderly people remained in Krajina, people who didn't want to leave their homes. He told us that around 600 such refugees were put up in our hotel, that there are other refugees in other hotels, and yet other refugees were placed in private homes. And he told us that Croatian authorities would have this problem with Martic and SAO Krajina, because as person number 3 put it, all this was the result of the crimes of Martic and his police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So did person number 10 tell you why these refugees, these Croat refugees, had left the area of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told us about some cases where people were forced out, expelled. Other people had got into trouble with Martic's police. They were beaten up. Yet other people had their cattle poisoned, properties ruined. And then he suggested that we talk to the refugees ourselves to hear it from them, and that seemed indeed the best idea, because we could not ignore the problems of the refugees. And one of my colleagues and I decided to interview the refugees to find out why they had left their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before that happened, did you meet with Milan Martic and talk to him about this -- these refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Milan Martic and talk to him about these refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. After interviewing the refugees, after number 3 and number 11 and I had this meeting with the refugees in the conference room of the hotel where we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, then let's take it in order. Let's talk about that meeting that you had with the refugees first and I'll ask you questions about your meeting with Milan Martic. So the meeting with the refugees in the conference room of the hotel, could you describe what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since number 10, together with number 11, organised and prepared this meeting with the refugees, we were told that the meeting would take place that day or the next day around 15 or 1600 hours in the conference room of that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many refugees would you say came to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 350 or 400 people attended that meeting. I can only assume that that was the number, because that was the capacity of the room. Most of those people were young, and some of them had brought children with them because they had no one to leave them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the refugees or some of the refugees tell you what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Person number 3 was supposed to be the moderator of that meeting. However, the refugees insisted that I be the moderator instead. A number of them told us about the various reasons that made them flee from that region, mainly Knin, because most of them were from Knin. At first, seven or eight young people, 30-ish or so, took off their clothes showing traces of beatings and explained that the Martic's -- the Martic police force had beaten them, and I saw the bruises on their bodies, but I couldn't help them much at that moment except to advise them to try to get damages through courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that they responded that the situation was one of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, the -- these seven or eight young people, you say they took off their clothes. Did they take off all of their clothes or just part of their clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some stripped to the waist, some would just roll up their shirts or T-shirts, because it was summer and it was warm. Enough for us to see that they had been beaten. They had some bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were these seven or eight young people, were they all men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you just say where on their bodies, if you can remember, did you see the bruises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly above the waist, on the back, and on the upper arms above the elbow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after these seven or eight men showed you their bruises, did other refugees tell you anything about what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other refugees gave us -- told us their stories. I had my notes from that meeting somewhere that I used later in writing up my report. They said that Serbs and Martic's men had cut their orchards. One or two people said that their pigs or chicken had been poisoned. Yet others said that they were Martic's neighbours, and they used to be on good terms with him and his family, but lately when they would ask him for help, he would respond that they shouldn't expect anything, and if they could live by the laws of SAO Krajina then they could stay, but if not, they should go. There was no room for them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did any of the refugees talk about encounters with Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them said that they had encounters with Martic himself, that his men had beaten them. Yes, there were a few such individuals. But it was a large crowd at that meeting, and they were beginning to talk at the same time. Everybody was eager to tell their own story. And we were frantically trying to take notes and tried to find out eventually what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did any -- any of the refugees talk about anything that had happened to their houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several people said that their houses had been burnt down by Martic's men. They said it was done as revenge because they were Croats, because they didn't want to live in SAO Krajina, that they maintained they were citizens of Croatia, and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did any of the refugees talk about Martic's Police coming to their houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases of that kind. Several people said that Martic's policemen went door-to-door telling people to leave Knin, that is the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The notes that you have referred to that you took at this meeting, what happened to those notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I moderated that meeting together with my colleague, number 3, we wrote a report that same day, on three pages, I think, and submitted it to person number 2, who was supposed to pass it on to our government in Belgrade. What was later on about it I really can't tell you, because my job ended with submitting that report. I did ask to be kept informed, and he did tell me that he had to go to army headquarters and send the report to Belgrade from there. So I don't know what was eventually sent, whether some amendments were made to what we wrote, but we wrote the report in hand and signed it. We had no other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after you -- after you wrote that report and submitted it, what happened to the notes that you had taken at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were all armed with writing pads and pencils when we went to those meetings. Not only with the refugees, but throughout my stay in Knin I constantly took notes in that writing pad, which I took with me when I went back to Belgrade. I used it later on my visits to Slavonia and Baranja, and later when I visited Doboj. And that writing pad with Official Notes that were confidential was kept in my office in Belgrade until the moment when the building was taken over by the Secretariat of the Interior of the republic. And I lost my entire desk including the contents, including the writing pad. All the other things in my drawers were personal effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting that you had with the refugees, did you have a meeting with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, as agreed with person number 2 -- I think it was with person number 3, but I'm sorry, I cannot be quite sure. We went to see Martic. I think I was with person number 3, because we had attended those meetings together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you talk to Milan Martic about the refugees who had appeared in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day, Milan Martic received us, and we had talks with him in his office touching upon the issue of refugees, which was in fact the main point we intended to raise that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say about these refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, we spoke first telling him about the meeting that we had had with the refugees and the reasons they had given us for leaving their homes and fleeing. In fact, I conveyed to Martic all that I had heard from refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His reaction was first to reject all these allegations as untrue and incorrect. He said these are all mothers, brothers, sisters, fathers, sons, whose family members were parts of the ZNG and the Ustasha units, as I said, that they were on the Croatian side against the Serbs, that all of them had a family member who was that. Then he said that they all refused to obey the laws of the SAO Krajina and that they did not want to live with the Serbs. He said they were all pro-Ustasha, that they were all hostile to the Serbs. I think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did he -- well, before I ask that question, let me ask this: Did he -- did you specifically tell him about observing injuries on some of the refugees and, if so, did he have any reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-079 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him about everything from the meeting. As for the injuries, he said, "Well, they can injure themselves, inflict injuries on themselves and then show this and say that somebody had beaten them." He said Martic's Police beat no one without a reason. When I said about the orchards that had been cut down, he said, "They cut them down themselves in order to blame Martic's men." When I said that five or six houses had been torched, he said, "Well, everybody knows what houses were torched, the houses of those who were directly members of the ZNG or leaders of the ZNG." When I told him that he had caused fights among neighbours, he said, "That's what they say. I told them if they wanted to stay they could stay, but anyone to stayed had to respect the laws of the SAO Krajina." He said they rejected that and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
